title: Your agent remembers. Can it finish the job?
description: A visual journey through six 2026 papers on agent memory, experience, handoffs, knowledge-graph retrieval and recovery, with illustrated examples and links to the research.
intro: A trip request sounds simple. Then a rule changes, a fact is missing or a search fails. Can the agent keep working?
stakes: If it loses the thread, you repeat yourself, wait or start over.
byline: A research journey with Pratyay Banerjee and collaborators.
hero_alt: An airplane wing above the clouds frames an illustrative trip-planning story.
scope: Illustrative trip story; the papers have separate experiments. Four papers are in 2026 proceedings. Two November arXiv papers report acceptance to Findings of EACL 2027, whose proceedings are forthcoming.

steps.label: APEX-MEM
steps.question: It remembered. The wrong version.
steps.problem: Use an old preference and you suggest the wrong flight. Erase it and you lose the history of what changed.
steps.idea: Keep dated memories. Resolve changing information when answering, rather than overwriting the history.
steps.example: Keep both the earlier evening-flight preference and the current morning-flight preference. Retrieve the one that fits the question's time.
steps.alt: Two illustrated boarding passes show an earlier evening preference at 9 PM and a current morning preference at 8 AM. A timeline retains both versions.

steps.label: APEX-EM
steps.question: The same dead end. Again.
steps.problem: Without reusable experience, each trip starts from scratch. Useful steps get rediscovered. Failed attempts get repeated.
steps.idea: Store successful and failed task attempts. Retrieve useful experience for the next task without retraining the model.
steps.example: Bring useful flight-search steps forward, along with the record of an expired link that led nowhere.
steps.alt: An illustrated open travel notebook records useful search steps on one page and failed attempts on the other.

steps.label: WK-Drift
steps.question: A useful plan. Until the rules change.
steps.problem: A saved procedure can look right and still be out of date. Which stored plans now need maintenance?
steps.idea: Benchmark how an agent maintains stored plans after known changes to facts or procedures. Identify affected plans, then update them.
steps.example: A supplied travel-rule update affects the rule-checking plan. The separate price-comparison plan stays unchanged.
steps.alt: A revised travel document connects to two stored-plan folders. An unaffected price plan is kept; an affected travel-rule plan is updated.

steps.label: Routed Graph Handoff
steps.question: The next agent joins. Does the context make it?
steps.problem: A handoff is useful only if the next agent can act on it. The format of the brief is part of the problem.
steps.idea: Choose a structured map of steps or a plain-language brief for each task. The receiving agent must be able to execute the chosen format.
steps.example: A planner briefs a search agent using either connected Search, Check and Compare steps, or instructions in plain language.
steps.alt: Planner and search-agent icons exchange context. Two alternative briefs show a map of connected steps and the same instructions in plain language.

steps.label: Graph-guided search
steps.question: The link you need. Buried in search results.
steps.problem: Matching words can miss a useful connection. Expanding every graph neighbor can add more noise.
steps.idea: Plan the knowledge-graph traversal. Look up one relationship at a time, use newly discovered names to retrieve passages, and ground the answer in text.
steps.example: Follow a city's served-by relationship to an airport, then use that airport name to find supporting text.
steps.alt: An illustrated city connects to an airport through a served-by relationship. The discovered name guides targeted text retrieval and an evidence-supported answer.

steps.label: Agent-Kernel
steps.question: One price check fails. Why start over?
steps.problem: Restart the whole task and you repeat completed calls. That means more waiting and more wasted work.
steps.idea: Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR) retries failed work and the steps that depend on it, while keeping unrelated completed results.
steps.example: Retry Vendor A's failed price check. Keep completed results from Vendors B and C, then compare once all three are ready.
steps.alt: An airport-style price-check board shows Vendor A failed and retrying, while completed results from Vendors B and C are kept.
